name: Narcissism Test
tagline: See where you fall on the spectrum of narcissistic traits.
intro: Everyone has some narcissistic traits, and a healthy dose of self-confidence is useful. This screener looks at five areas: grandiosity, entitlement, need for admiration, empathy and fragile self-esteem. Answer honestly based on how you usually think and feel. It takes about five minutes and is not a diagnosis, but it shows where you fall on the spectrum.
seoTitle: Narcissism Test: Free narcissistic traits screener
seoDescription: How narcissistic are you really? Take this 5-minute test on grandiosity, entitlement, admiration, empathy and self-esteem and get a personal report.

grandiosity.name: Grandiosity
grandiosity.short: How strongly you see yourself as special, superior or destined for greatness.
grandiosity.low: Your answers suggest that you have a modest, realistic view of yourself. You do not seem to see yourself as superior to others or destined for special greatness. This makes you approachable and easy to work with. Just make sure modesty does not turn into underselling yourself: recognising your real strengths helps you take on challenges and opportunities with confidence.
grandiosity.mid: Your answers suggest a healthy level of self-confidence with some belief in your special abilities. You probably trust your talents and have ambitions, which can drive success. At times you may overestimate yourself a little, as most people do. Asking for honest feedback and staying curious about what others do well keeps your confidence grounded and your relationships balanced, and helps you keep growing.
grandiosity.high: Your answers suggest that you strongly see yourself as exceptional, superior or destined for greatness. Confidence like this can fuel ambition, but it can also lead to disappointment, conflict or blind spots when reality does not match the picture. Try to test your self-image against concrete feedback. If these beliefs cause problems in your relationships or work, consider talking to a qualified professional, who can help you explore them without judgement.

entitlement.name: Entitlement
entitlement.short: How much you expect special treatment or feel others should meet your needs.
entitlement.low: Your answers suggest that you rarely expect special treatment and readily accept the same rules as everyone else. You seem to appreciate what others do for you and take responsibility for your actions. These qualities build trust and goodwill. Remember that it is still fine to ask for what you need and to stand up for yourself when you are treated unfairly.
entitlement.mid: Your answers suggest that you sometimes feel you deserve more than you get, or become annoyed when things do not go your way. This is quite common, especially when you work hard. Notice when frustration turns into expecting others to adapt to you. Expressing gratitude and seeing things from the other person's side can help keep your expectations fair and your relationships warm and balanced.
entitlement.high: Your answers suggest that you often expect special treatment, feel others should meet your needs and become frustrated when they do not. This pattern can strain relationships and lead to repeated conflicts or disappointment. It helps to ask yourself what you are giving in return and how others might see the situation. If this pattern causes difficulties, consider talking to a qualified professional who can help you understand where these expectations come from.

admiration.name: Need for admiration
admiration.short: How much you seek attention, praise and recognition from others.
admiration.low: Your answers suggest that you do not need much attention or praise to feel good about yourself. You are comfortable in the background and let others shine. This inner independence is a real strength. Just make sure your achievements are visible when it matters, for example at work, as others cannot appreciate what they do not see. Sharing your successes now and then is not bragging; it simply keeps people informed.
admiration.mid: Your answers suggest that you enjoy attention and recognition, while not being entirely dependent on it. Wanting to be appreciated is perfectly human. Pay attention to moments when you seek praise to soothe insecurity rather than to share joy. Building satisfaction from your own values and progress, not only from reactions, makes your self-esteem more stable and less dependent on the mood of the people around you.
admiration.high: Your answers suggest that attention, praise and admiration are very important to how you feel about yourself. When recognition is missing, you may feel hurt, empty or restless. Relying heavily on outside approval can make self-esteem fragile and relationships one-sided. Try to notice what you value in yourself regardless of others' reactions. If this need feels hard to manage, consider exploring it with a qualified professional, such as a therapist.

empathy_deficit.name: Low empathy
empathy_deficit.short: How hard it is for you to tune in to and care about other people's feelings.
empathy_deficit.low: Your answers suggest that you tune in to other people's feelings and care about how your actions affect them. You seem to listen well and notice when someone needs support. Empathy is one of the strongest foundations for close relationships. Make sure you also leave room for your own needs, so caring for others does not drain you. Healthy empathy includes setting limits when you need them.
empathy_deficit.mid: Your answers suggest that your empathy is present but varies. When you are busy, stressed or focused on your own goals, other people's feelings may fade into the background. Try to pause and ask how someone is really doing, and listen without immediately advising or judging. Small gestures of understanding, such as remembering what matters to someone, make a big difference in relationships.
empathy_deficit.high: Your answers suggest that tuning in to others' feelings, or caring about how your actions affect them, is often difficult for you. Others may experience you as distant or dismissive, which can lead to conflicts and loneliness. Empathy can be strengthened through practice, such as listening without interrupting and asking about others' experiences. If this pattern affects your relationships, consider talking to a qualified professional who can support you in exploring it.

vulnerability.name: Fragile self-esteem
vulnerability.short: How sensitive your self-esteem is to criticism, rejection and comparison.
vulnerability.low: Your answers suggest that your self-esteem is fairly stable. Criticism, mistakes or other people's success do not seem to shake your sense of worth much. This security allows you to learn from feedback and enjoy others' achievements. Keep treating setbacks as information rather than as verdicts on who you are. This calm, secure attitude also makes it easier for others to be open and honest with you.
vulnerability.mid: Your answers suggest that your self-esteem is sometimes affected by criticism, rejection or comparison. You may feel hurt more than you show, or brood after a slight. This is very common. Try to separate feedback on what you did from judgements about who you are, and talk about hurt feelings with someone you trust instead of hiding them. Sharing vulnerability often brings people closer.
vulnerability.high: Your answers suggest that beneath the surface your self-esteem may be quite fragile: criticism, rejection or others' success can hit hard and trigger shame, envy or anger. This vulnerable side of narcissistic traits is often painful and hidden from others. Please be kind to yourself, as this sensitivity usually has understandable roots. Consider talking to a qualified professional, who can help you build a steadier, more secure sense of self-worth.

summary: Narcissistic traits exist on a spectrum, and everyone has some of them. This report shows where you fall on five areas, from confident grandiosity to fragile self-esteem. Higher scores mean stronger traits. The results are not a diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder; only a qualified professional can assess that.
